name: pengyhash
workload: SMHasher bulk speed test: 262144-byte keys, averaged over byte alignments 0-7
claimed_speedup: 13347.17 MiB/s vs 11176.72 MiB/s for xxHash64, ~19% faster (derived from page data)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 3350G 3.6GHz (rurban/smhasher default reference machine, per README)
stars_or_usage: 12 stars (tinypeng/pengyhash); packaged as a reference hash in rurban/smhasher (2.2k stars)
tradeoffs: 64-bit output only, no seeding beyond a 32-bit seed, GPLv3 license (copyleft, unlike most peer non-crypto hashes which are permissive)
caveats: Speed figure comes from the independent rurban/smhasher shootout table, not pengyhash's own repo (which has no benchmark section); compiler and optimization flags used for the shootout are not stated, only CPU model and GHz, so tier is capped at B.
found_via: vcpkg ports tree scan for *hash* -> ports/murmurhash -> aappleby/smhasher -> rurban/smhasher (active fork) README speed/quality table

name: SpookyHash (SpookyV2)
workload: SMHasher bulk speed test: 262144-byte keys, averaged over byte alignments 0-7 (SpookyV2_64 variant)
claimed_speedup: 13401.13 MiB/s vs 11176.72 MiB/s for xxHash64, ~20% faster (derived from page data)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 3350G 3.6GHz (rurban/smhasher default reference machine, per README)
stars_or_usage: 72 stars (this thread-safe/multi-endian mirror); original design by Bob Jenkins, historically used in Redis modules, FoundationDB and Blizzard's Battle.net
tradeoffs: Larger/more complex implementation than xxHash or wyhash; original reference lives on Bob Jenkins' personal page (burtleburtle.net/bob/hash/spooky.html) rather than a maintained repo -- this GitHub mirror is itself archived.
caveats: Repo is GitHub-archived (read-only); speed numbers are from the independent smhasher shootout, not the repo's own benchmarks. Compiler/flags for the shootout are unstated (CPU model only), so tier capped at B.
found_via: gh search repos 'spookyhash' -> g1mv/spookyhash; cross-checked bulk speed against rurban/smhasher SpookyV2_64 result page

name: NMHASH (NMHASH32X)
workload: SMHasher3 bulk speed test: 262144-byte keys, averaged over byte alignments 0-7, AVX2 build
claimed_speedup: 25.44 GiB/s (NMHASH) vs 13.02 GiB/s (XXH-64) and 15.52 GiB/s (CityHash-64) on the same run -- ~95% faster than xxHash64, ~64% faster than CityHash64 (derived from page data)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, isolated CPU pinned to 3.5GHz, boost disabled (fwojcik/smhasher3 reference machine, per README)
stars_or_usage: 7 stars (gzm55/hash-garage collection); NMHASH itself is also bundled directly inside rurban/smhasher and fwojcik/smhasher3
tradeoffs: 32-bit output hash (NMHASH32/NMHASH32X), AVX2 build used for the fastest numbers reported here; scalar path is slower; small/obscure repo with little independent adoption outside the smhasher test suites.
caveats: Same-run comparison against XXH-64 and CityHash-64 was pulled from fwojcik/smhasher3's per-hash result files (independent, actively maintained fork of smhasher); CPU and compiler version are stated but exact compile flags are not, capping tier at B. NMHASH64 is close to but does not clearly beat wyhash (25.44 vs 23.17 GiB/s) or XXH3 (42.21 GiB/s) in the same run.
found_via: gh search code 'nmhash' across GitHub -> fwojcik/smhasher3 hashes/nmhash.cpp -> canonical implementation at gzm55/hash-garage; results/raw/NMHASH.txt, XXH-64.txt, CityHash-64.txt in fwojcik/smhasher3

name: rustc-hash (FxHash)
workload: General-purpose hashing of compiler data structures (integers, short strings/slices) inside rustc's internal hash maps/sets
claimed_speedup: "speedy" / faster than SipHash for the compiler's workload; no numbers given in the repo
stars_or_usage: 597 stars; 827M+ downloads on crates.io; used as the internal hasher (FxHashMap/FxHashSet) throughout the rustc compiler itself
tradeoffs: Not DoS-resistant (unsuitable for untrusted-input hash maps, unlike SipHash); current algorithm is a polynomial hash with a wyhash-inspired string compression step, not the original 'FxHash' bit-mix despite the crate keeping that name for compatibility.
caveats: No quantitative benchmark or methodology is published in the repo/README -- purely a first-party qualitative claim ('hashing speed is critical... we prefer a quicker algorithm'). Counted per the rules as at most one Tier D entry this run because of its scale of real-world usage (rustc itself, 827M downloads).
found_via: crates.io API q=hash&sort=downloads -> rustc-hash crate (#9 by downloads) -> rust-lang/rustc-hash repo README
